description:
A heavy-bodied, dark dabbler that closely matches the mallard's structural footprint, sporting soot-brown body plumage that contrasts sharply with a pale grayish-buff head and neck. In flight, the species shows brilliant, silvery-white underwings that flash against the dark body, and a deep violet-purple speculum that lacks the white border bars found on mallards, though it occasionally carries a faint black trailing edge. Drakes carry bright olive-yellow bills, while hens display duller greenish-olive bills mottled with dusky flecks.

Highly athletic, they burst nearly straight up off salt-marsh tidal creeks and blackwater sloughs with powerful, whistling wing strokes. Their flight silhouette is identical to the mallard, but the stark contrast between the bright silver underwing lining and dark body provides instant long-range identification. The hen's vocalization is a loud, ringing quack virtually indistinguishable from a hen mallard, while the drake provides a low, reedy groan.

Widely considered the wariest duck in eastern marshes, they circle high outside spreads for multiple passes, requiring complete blind concealment, low-profile hides, and zero calling once they begin their final swing. Decoys must be kept entirely free of frost, mud, and unnatural shine, as these birds flare at the slightest visual irregularity. Because of localized population pressures and restrictive single-bird or two-bird bag limits across the Atlantic and Mississippi flyways, careful aerial differentiation from mottled ducks and hen mallards is critical.
lifespan: 5–10 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; aquatic plants, seeds, grains, insects, mollusks, and crustaceans
habitat: Salt marshes, beaver ponds, forested wetlands, and coastal estuaries
conservation_status: Least Concern (Population monitored closely due to hunting and habitat loss)

description: This monomorphic bird is a plump, rounded waterbird with slate-gray to dark charcoal body plumage, a black head and neck, dark red eyes, and large, greenish-gray feet equipped with broad, flattened swimming lobes instead of webbing. Its bill is stark white with a tiny brown spot near the tip and a small brown frontal callus on the forehead. The tail is short and carried low while swimming, often giving the bird a rounded, chicken-like profile on open water. To become airborne, they require long, pattering runs across open water while furiously beating their short, rounded wings. In flight, they show a thin, whitish trailing edge on the secondaries and fly with rapid, labored wing strokes, dragging their large feet behind their tail. They vocalize with sharp, metallic croaks and grunts, frequently chattering when gathered in large rafts. Often rafts in thousands on open lakes and coastal bays, feeding on submerged vegetation alongside diving ducks. They are readily distinguished from game ducks by their chicken-like head-bobbing swimming motion and chalk-white bills, making early-morning identification simple. While many waterfowlers overlook them, they are traditionally pursued in southern marshes for use in hearty stews and gumbos.
lifespan: 8–9 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; aquatic vegetation, algae, seeds, insects, and small fish
habitat: Freshwater lakes, marshes, ponds, and slow rivers

description:
North America's smallest dabbling duck, drakes sport a rich chestnut-red head with a broad, iridescent emerald-green eye stripe, a vertical white crescent on the shoulder, and a creamy, buff-colored patch beneath the tail. The speculum on both sexes is a vivid, shimmering green bordered by buffy-tan bars, set against an overall dark, compact wing. Hens are cryptically mottled brown with small, dark bills and pale bellies.

Flocks fly at breakneck speeds just inches above the water or marsh grass, executing breathtaking, synchronized twists, dives, and banks like a flock of sandpipers. They drop suddenly into decoy spreads without warning, pitching straight downward with wings cupped. Drakes produce a high-pitched, cricket-like bell whistle transcribed as "krick-et" or "peep", while hens deliver brief, rapid, high-pitched quacks.

Extremely hardy early-and-late migrants that favor very shallow water, muddy edges, and ankle-deep sheetwater in flooded agricultural fields. Because their diminutive size makes them appear further away than they actually are, hunters should use open chokes such as improved cylinder or light modified paired with smaller shot sizes like #5 or #6 steel. Decoy spreads can be kept compact, and simple teal whistling calls are often enough to draw circling flocks into gun range.
lifespan: 5–10 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous and insectivorous; seeds, aquatic plants, and aquatic insects
habitat: Shallow marshes, flooded agricultural fields, ponds, and mudflats

description:
Known as the "baldpate," the breeding drake features a striking white crown stripe, an iridescent dark green patch extending back from the eye, a short blue-gray bill with a black tip, and pinkish-brown flanks. In flight, both sexes show a bright white belly that contrasts sharply with a dark chest, and mature drakes show massive, snow-white forewing shoulder patches visible at great distances. Hens are warm grayish-brown with contrasting white bellies and duller gray forewing coverts.

Flocks fly in rapid, erratic bunches that bank, pivot, and weave tightly like shorebirds, often dipping low over the marsh before climbing steeply. Their wing cadence is quick and nervous, creating a distinct visual flutter when approaching water. The flight is constantly vocal: drakes produce a distinct, breathy three-note whistle sounding like "whee-whee-whoo" with the accent on the middle note, while hens give a low, growling "qurrr".

Aggressive feeders nicknamed "poachers" for stealing submerged aquatic grasses from diving canvasbacks and coots in open water. They decoy readily to dedicated wigeon whistles and large spreads placed over shallow, grassy flats, but their erratic aerial maneuvers require disciplined lead and follow-through. Placing confidence coot decoys or canvasback blocks alongside a dabbler rig is a proven way to draw wary baldpates into the pocket.
lifespan: 6–10 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; aquatic plants, algae, grasses, and agricultural crops
habitat: Freshwater marshes, lakes, agricultural fields, and coastal bays

description:
A small, compact marine goose displaying a solid jet-black head, neck, and upper chest, contrasting with a barred grayish-brown back, a pale whitish belly, and a thin, broken white necklace marking the mid-neck. Their bills and legs are black, and the tail is framed by bright white upper and lower coverts. Their overall body mass is only slightly larger than a heavy mallard, giving them an exceptionally compact profile on open water.

Flies in long, undulating ribbons or low, wavering chains that skim inches above open saltwater bays and flats, propelled by rapid, stiff wing strokes. Their flight pattern rarely climbs to significant altitudes when traveling locally between feeding shoals and roosting waters. Their vocalization is a low, rolling, guttural purr or croak sounding like "r-r-r-oook", which carries across coastal sounds and sounds entirely distinct from the honk of a Canada goose.

Strongly tied to intertidal eelgrass (Zostera marina) and sea lettuce beds along the Atlantic coast from New Jersey to Virginia. They are traditional coastal game that decoy willingly to specialized low-profile shoreline hides and floating silhouette or block spreads placed over shallow tidal shoals. Hunters must plan their outings around outgoing tides when birds move actively toward exposed eelgrass flats.
lifespan: 10–15 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; eelgrass, sea lettuce, algae, and salt-marsh grasses
habitat: Marine bays, saltwater estuaries, mudflats, and eelgrass beds

description: This monomorphic bird is a large, robust woodland pigeon with a slate-blue and purplish-gray body, a long, rounded tail marked with a wide, pale gray terminal band, and a bright yellow bill tipped in black. Mature birds display an iridescent bronze-green nape patch topped by a clean, narrow white crescent across the back of the neck. Legs and feet are bright yellow, offering a distinct visual contrast against their dark slate plumage. Swift, direct, and powerful fliers that flush from high timber canopies with loud, clapping wingbeats, navigating mountain canyons and forest breaks at speeds exceeding forty-five miles per hour. Their flight paths are arrow-straight and purposeful as they traverse between high roosting ridges and feeding benches. They produce deep, owl-like cooing, but they remain almost completely silent while traveling on the wing. Found in mature oak, Douglas fir, and pine forests across western mountains, feeding heavily on wild acorns, elderberries, and cascara berries. Hunters set up along high mountain passes, canyon saddles, or mineral springs, pass-shooting fast-crossing birds that require substantial forward leads and tight chokes. Shell limits are often strictly enforced in western states, making ammunition conservation and target selection vital.
lifespan: Up to 14 years in the wild
diet: Granivorous and frugivorous; acorns, berries, pine seeds, and grain
habitat: Coniferous and deciduous mountain forests, oak woodlands, and forest edges

description:
A medium-sized sea duck; mature drakes are entirely jet-black from bill to tail, highlighted by a bulbous, swollen, bright yellow-orange knob at the base of the bill. Hens and immature birds are dark soot-brown with a clean, contrasting two-toned head pattern featuring pale buffy-white cheeks below a dark crown. Both sexes display completely dark wings above and below that flash silvery along the flight feathers in bright sunlight.

Travels in large, shifting, shapeless flocks that track wave troughs low over the ocean, driven by continuous, stiff wing propulsion. Their flight lines hug the contours of heavy surf, rarely climbing high unless crossing over barrier beach points. Drakes produce a melodious, mournful whistling note sounding like "cour-lee", which has earned them the traditional coastal moniker of "butterbills".

Concentrated along ocean surf zones, outer barrier beaches, and large open sounds, feeding extensively on small blue mussels and mollusks. Decoying them requires longline spreads equipped with large, high-contrast black decoys set into open-water tidal cuts. Their heavy muscle structure and dense plumage necessitate heavy non-toxic shot payloads like #2 or #1 steel, along with prompt follow-up shots on swimming birds.
lifespan: 8–12 years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous; marine mollusks, crustaceans, and small fish
habitat: Coastal marine waters, ocean bays, and surf zones
nesting_season: June to July (Arctic tundra near freshwater)
conservation_status: Near Threatened / Least Concern (Vulnerable to marine oil spills)

description:
A tall, long-legged waterfowl with an upright, goose-like posture, featuring a bright coral-pink to orange-red bill, a rich chestnut breast and back, a dark brown cap, and a stark black belly. In flight, the upper wings display an unmistakable, massive white band running the entire length of the wing coverts, contrasting against black primary and secondary flight feathers. Sexes are visually identical in plumage and bare-part coloration throughout the entire season.

Flocks fly with slow, buoyant, shallow wing strokes, trailing their long pink legs noticeably past their short tails. Their flight posture appears somewhat hunched, with broad, rounded wings providing significant lift in heavy air. They are intensely vocal in flight, filling the air with continuous, high-pitched, multi-note whistling calls transcribed as "pe-che-che-ne", which makes approaching flocks audible long before they appear through the blind grass.

Expanding steadily northward through southern agricultural landscapes, flooded rice impoundments, and stock ponds. They fly in large, noisy groups that commit eagerly to stationary puddle duck spreads without calling, often perching readily on blind frames, dead timber, or fence lines. Their meat is highly regarded for table use, featuring a mild, sweet flavor comparable to prime field-fed dabblers.
lifespan: Up to 10+ years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; seeds, grains, aquatic vegetation, and insects
habitat: Shallow freshwater ponds, flooded agricultural fields, wooded swamps, and rice paddies

description:
A small, nimble dabbler, the drake is distinguished in breeding plumage by a slate-blue head with a prominent white crescent between the bill and eye, spotted pinkish-tan flanks, and a white flank patch near the tail. In flight, both sexes display huge, chalky powder-blue upper wing coverts separated from an iridescent green speculum by a white border strip. Hens are mottled grayish-brown with dark eyelines, carrying the same prominent blue wing patches.

Highly coordinated, flashing flight groups that buzz low over emergent vegetation, banking sharply in unison to expose the chalk-blue shoulder panels. They fly with tremendous speed, often banking hard into the wind and touching down in decoy pockets on the very first pass. Drakes emit a faint, high-pitched peeping whistle, while females produce a series of light, nasal, rapid quacks.

The earliest migrant among continental waterfowl, heading south to the Gulf Coast and Central America at the first sign of cool weather in late August and September. They are the primary species pursued during special early teal seasons, where their rapid flight speeds and tendency to bomb decoys on the first pass require fast gun mounts. Hunters should deploy small spreads of hen mallard or teal decoys in shallow, vegetated impoundments, using open chokes to handle fast crossing shots.
lifespan: Up to 10 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; seeds, aquatic plants, aquatic insects, and snails
habitat: Shallow marshes, ponds, flooded ditches, and grassy wetlands

description: This monomorphic bird is distinguished from the Atlantic race by its much darker appearance, carrying an almost complete, broad white collar encircling the upper neck and a very dark, brownish-black breast and belly that blends smoothly into the black neck. The back is dark slaty-brown, and the white undertail coverts form a sharp, clean contrast against the dark belly plumage. Flocks skim intertidal sandbars and ocean estuaries in shifting, wave-like formations, displaying swift, synchronized turns as they approach feeding flats. They fly with stiff, shallow wingbeats, maintaining tight group spacing just above the breakers. They emit the same low, resonant, rolling guttural growl on the wing as their Atlantic cousins, creating a low murmur across coastal bays. Dependent on tidal eelgrass flats along the Pacific rim from Alaska to Baja California. Successful hunting requires intercepting birds as rising tides float eelgrass leaves or as falling tides expose feeding shoals, setting up low blinds on exposed points. Hunters should place dark silhouette or floating brant decoys on exposed gravel spits, keeping profiles low to blend into the barren coastal environment.
lifespan: 10–15 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; intertidal eelgrass, marine algae, and salt-marsh plants
habitat: Coastal marine estuaries, sandbars, mudflats, and protected bays

description:
North America's smallest diving duck, the drake is instantly recognized by an oversized, puffy head with a massive, brilliant white wedge extending from behind the eye across the crown, set against iridescent purple-green plumage. The body is bright white along the flanks and breast with a dark black back; hens are compact, dark brownish-gray with a distinct, neat white oval cheek patch. Both sexes have small gray bills and pale pinkish-gray feet.

Unlike most diving ducks, buffleheads can leap directly off the water into full flight without running, flying low, fast, and straight with buzzy, rapid wingbeats. They travel in pairs or small groups of five to ten birds, maintaining a steady, low-altitude heading. They are generally silent on the wing, though hens emit a weak, low-pitched quack when flushed off small ponds.

Common along sheltered bays, tidal creeks, and farm ponds, often diving in synchronized patterns to feed on small mollusks and aquatic insects. They decoy aggressively to any spread with bright white paint, but their small size and speed demand sharp shooting, and downed birds must be retrieved immediately because of their ability to dive deep when crippled. Hunters can use small, specialized spreads set close to shorelines, as buffleheads rarely demand large, open-water longline setups.
lifespan: Up to 7–10 years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous; aquatic insects, crustaceans, mollusks, and small fish
habitat: Sheltered coastal bays, estuaries, lakes, ponds, and slow rivers
nesting_season: May to July (often in abandoned woodpecker cavities)

description:
Formerly classified as a small Canada goose subspecies, this distinct species is roughly the size of a large mallard, featuring a noticeably short neck, a steep forehead, and a tiny, stubby triangular bill. Plumage mimics the Canada goose pattern with a black neck, white cheek patches, and a brown body, though some individuals carry a faint white collar at the base of the neck. Their breast coloration ranges from light gray to dark chocolate-brown depending on the subspecies.

Highly agile fliers that execute sudden banks, side-slips, and rolls into decoys with a high-tempo wingbeat cadence. Flocks move with a loose, erratic energy that allows them to dump out of the sky far more violently than large Canada geese. Instead of a deep honk, their vocalization is a high-pitched, squeaking cackle or yelp sounding like "yick-yick" or "cackle", which sounds more like a dog toy than a standard goose.

Winters in large concentrations in California, Texas, and the Pacific Northwest, often mixed in with larger geese in agricultural fields. Hunters must check regional regulations, as some areas enforce separate daily bag limits or closed zones specifically aimed at managing distinct cackler stocks. Decoy spreads should utilize specialized, smaller-bodied cackler decoys, and callers must tune their short-reed calls high to reproduce the squeaking cackle of incoming birds.
lifespan: 10–20+ years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; grasses, sedges, agricultural grains, and green shoots
habitat: Tundra, agricultural stubble fields, pastures, and marshlands

description: This monomorphic small cackling goose is recognized by a bold, wide white neck ring at the base of its black stocking neck, accentuated by a dark, chocolate-brown body and a steep, rounded forehead. Many individuals also display a distinct black line of feathers dividing the white cheek patches beneath the chin. Their overall frame is compact and stocky, resting on short black legs with a small, triangular bill. Displays swift, synchronized flock movements, flying in dense, shifting swarms over coastal pastures and river mouths with rapid, shallow wing beats. In the air, their maneuvers look remarkably nimble compared to larger geese, frequently side-slipping together on windy coastal approaches. Vocalizations are high-pitched, squeaking cackles delivered in rapid-fire succession that sound noticeably lighter and higher than a standard honker. A historic conservation success story, this subspecies recovered from near-extinction caused by introduced predators on its Aleutian nesting islands. Today, they winter in large concentrations along coastal Oregon and northern California, where specialized harvest zones manage them while preventing overharvest on localized staging pastures. Hunters setting spreads over coastal ryegrass fields must confirm current regional quotas to remain compliant with designated harvest caps.
lifespan: 10–25 years in the wild (up to 40 years in captivity)
diet: Herbivorous; grasses, sedges, roots, berries, and agricultural grains
habitat: Coastal pastures, tidal flats, tundra, and agricultural fields
conservation_status: Recovered / Least Concern (Delisted from US Endangered Species Act)

description:
A large, familiar wild goose featuring a gray-brown body, a long black stocking neck, an all-black head, and a wide white cheek patch extending beneath the chin. The bill and legs are black, and the tail is dark, framed by a clean white U-shaped rump patch. Size varies across subspecies, but true Canada geese are substantial, heavy-bodied birds with broad wing spans and prominent chest structures.

Flocks travel in disciplined, iconic V-formations or long, undulating lines, driven by powerful, rhythmic wingbeats. When approaching fields, they circle deliberately, locking their wide wings and backpedaling firmly into the wind on final descent. They are intensely vocal on the wing, communicating across long distances with deep, resonant, two-syllable honks sounding like "ah-honk", where the higher pitched note is given by the female and the lower note by the male.

The cornerstone of field and water goose hunting across North America, feeding heavily in harvested corn, wheat, barley, and pasture fields. Fooled using realistic full-body decoy spreads, disciplined calling routines, and layout or A-frame blinds that conceal hunters from overhead scrutiny. Flagging is essential for grabbing the attention of distant migrating flights, but flags should be rested once birds turn and commit to the final approach.
lifespan: 10–24 years in the wild (record over 30 years)
diet: Herbivorous; grasses, grains, roots, and aquatic plants
habitat: Lakes, rivers, agricultural fields, city parks, and wetlands

description: A proportional, monomorphic, intermediate-sized Canada goose showing identical plumage patterns to Western Canadas, but built on a smaller frame with a shorter neck and a more compact bill. Body mass typically falls between five and seven pounds, resting squarely between large honkers and smaller cackling geese. Their plumage exhibits clean white cheek patches, a dark stocking neck, and light brownish-gray body feathering. Flocks fly in fast, agile formations that shift altitude rapidly in crosswinds, beating their wings with a noticeable increase in cadence compared to giant Canadas. Their honks are distinctly higher-pitched and faster than the booming notes of larger races, sounding energetic and urgent. When approaching fields, they tend to drop in large, swirling groups rather than small, orderly pairs. Abundant across the Central, Mississippi, and Pacific flyways, migrating in massive waves ahead of winter freezes to feed in grain stubble. They respond well to fast-paced short-reed calling and aggressive decoy flagging, often dumping into field spreads in large, chaotic packs. Hunters set out medium-sized full-body spreads mixed with windsocks to provide the volume needed to stop passing flocks.
lifespan: 10–20 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; grasses, agricultural grains, clover, and green shoots
habitat: Tundra, agricultural fields, river valleys, and wetlands

description: This monomorphic goose is among the largest recognized subspecies of Canada goose, often weighing ten to fourteen pounds, characterized by a massive bill, exceptionally long neck, and pale grayish-brown flanks. The plumage displays the classic white cheek patches and jet-black neck, but the overall coloration is noticeably lighter and washed-out compared to coastal races. Their large footprint and heavy wing structure give them a commanding appearance on field spreads. Flocks maintain slow, measured, and deliberate wing strokes, projecting immense power as they glide on cupped wings across western valleys and rivers. Their flight lines are steady and structured, rarely making the sudden erratic turns seen in smaller goose races. They voice deep, authoritative, booming honks that carry across wide agricultural basins, demanding respect from other approaching flocks. A staple of western agricultural regions and major river systems, feeding in alfalfa, wheat, and corn stubble. Because of their large size and cautious nature, hunters rely on oversized full-body decoys, realistic flagging to grab attention at a distance, and deep, resonant short-reed calling to finish them within range. Laying out on field edges with dialed-in camouflage is critical, as these mature honkers will circle repeatedly to inspect blind layouts.
lifespan: 10–25 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; agricultural grains, grasses, alfalfa, and clover
habitat: River valleys, agricultural fields, lakes, wetlands, and suburban turf

description:
The largest and fastest North American diving duck, defined by a long, heavy black bill that slopes seamlessly up into the forehead, creating a flat, wedge-shaped head profile. Breeding drakes display a rich copper-red head, red eyes, a jet-black breast, and a gleaming canvas-white back and body. Hens share the same distinctive sloping head profile but are rendered in soft grayish-brown and pale buff tones.

Renowned for raw speed, canvasbacks fly in powerful, unwavering V-formations or straight lines driven by rapid, stiff wing strokes. Their flight speed routinely exceeds fifty miles per hour, cutting across open water without the erratic banking seen in puddle ducks. Drakes produce a low, guttural croak or purr while resting on the water, but in flight, the species is predominantly silent, announced only by the distinct ripping sound of their wings cutting the air.

Bound to large open bays, lakes, and wide river channels rich in wild celery (Vallisneria americana), where their high flight speeds require aggressive forward leads and wide leads on crossing shots. Because of historical population fluctuations, they are strictly managed under restricted daily bag limits, often one or two birds, making quick profile recognition against Redheads essential. Oversized white-bodied decoys set on the upwind edge of a spread help steer these fast divers directly into the shooting lane.
lifespan: Up to 12–20 years in the wild
diet: Primarily herbivorous; tubers, roots, seeds of aquatic plants, and some mollusks
habitat: Large deep lakes, open bays, freshwater marshes, and slow rivers

description:
A western marsh specialist, the breeding drake is cloaked in rich, deep cinnamon-red across the head, neck, chest, and flanks, contrasted by bright crimson eyes and a long black spatulate bill. Their wing pattern is structurally identical to the blue-winged teal, sporting massive sky-blue shoulder coverts, a white separating bar, and an iridescent green speculum. Hens and eclipse drakes are mottled brown and almost indistinguishable in the field from female blue-winged teal, though they typically show a slightly longer, heavier bill.

Flies in small, darting groups that twist nimbly through dense stands of tules and bulrushes, dropping cleanly into small, isolated pockets of open water. Their wing action is light and rapid, allowing them to make immediate directional adjustments when navigating tight marsh channels. Drakes make low, rattling chatter calls sounding like "krr-krr-krr", while hens provide soft, weak quacks similar to blue-wings.

Bound primarily to the Pacific and Central flyways, frequenting warm alkaline wetlands, marsh margins, and sluggish agricultural canals. Fully plumaged drakes taken late in the season are among the most prized trophies for North American waterfowlers due to their striking color saturation. Hunting them requires setting up in shallow, protected marsh openings with small spreads of teal decoys, paying close attention to early morning flight corridors.
lifespan: 5–8 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; seeds, pondweeds, aquatic insects, and small crustaceans
habitat: Shallow freshwater marshes, ponds, and flooded agricultural areas
source: docx (image names from chat drafts, not yet confirmed)

description:
The heaviest and largest duck in the Northern Hemisphere, showing a distinctive long, sloping head with a heavy frontal shield feathering down the side of the long greenish-yellow bill. Prime drakes are white above and jet-black below, accented by an olive-green wash on the nape and a soft pinkish-peach wash on the chest. Hens are heavily barred in rich cinnamon-brown to protect them while nesting on rocky maritime islands.

Low-level, heavy fliers that cruise in long, stable, undulating lines skimming just inches above open ocean swells and wave troughs. Their wingbeats are measured and synchronized, holding steady flight paths even in gale-force ocean winds. Drakes vocalize with a strange, haunting, dove-like cooing sounding like "ah-ooh, ah-ooh", which carries across cold ocean sounds.

The defining quarry of coastal New England and eastern maritime waterfowlers, hunted from rocky shore blinds or specialized layout boats over mussel shoals. Their dense down, tough skin, and marine environment require specialized sea-duck decoy rigs anchored on heavy sinkers, dense non-toxic loads like sizes #1 to BB, and prompt follow-up shots on the water. Extreme care must be taken regarding ocean tides, freezing spray, and changing winter weather while targeting eiders offshore.
lifespan: 15–20+ years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous; marine mollusks, blue mussels, crustaceans, and sea urchins
habitat: Coastal marine waters, rocky islands, barrier reefs, and Arctic coastlines
source: docx (image names from chat drafts, not yet confirmed)

description: A monomorphic chicken-like wetland bird featuring dark charcoal-gray body plumage, white streaks along the flanks, white undertail coverts, and an unwebbed foot equipped with exceptionally long, slender green toes. It is instantly separated from the American Coot by its bright red frontal shield on the forehead and a matching red bill tipped with yellow. The body is laterally compressed, allowing it to walk through dense reeds without bending stems. Prefers swimming or walking over floating vegetation, taking to the air only when pressed by running across the water surface with rapid, shallow wing flutters. Once airborne, flight is labored and short, with long green legs dangling awkwardly behind the tail before the bird drops back into the weeds. They produce loud, laughing squawks and clucks from within dense cattail cover. Inhabits shallow freshwater marshes, swamps, and rice impoundments choked with lily pads and cattails. Harvested primarily on opportunistic passes during rail and snipe hunts, using the bright red frontal shield to distinguish them from coots and waterhens. Poling small skiffs through emergent marsh vegetation during flood tides provides the most reliable way to flush these secretive birds.
lifespan: 6–8 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; seeds, leaves, aquatic insects, snails, and small fish
habitat: Freshwater marshes, swamps, overgrown ponds, and flooded rice fields

description:
A medium-sized, cold-hardy diving duck, the drake features a puffy, triangular dark head glossed with bottle-green, a bright yellow eye, a black back, and an immaculate white circular spot positioned between the bill and the eye. Hens sport a chocolate-brown head, slate-gray body plumage, pale yellow eyes, and a bill that develops a yellow band across the tip late in the winter. In flight, both sexes show large, solid-white inner wing patches.

Known as "whistlers," their rapid, stiff wing strokes produce a distinct, high-pitched mechanical humming sound in flight that alerts hunters to their approach long before they are spotted visually. They fly in small, fast groups, cutting direct lines close to open water surfaces. In flight, they rarely vocalize, relying almost entirely on their whistling wings for flock coordination.

Among the last waterfowl to push south in the winter, moving only when northern lakes and rivers completely freeze over. They are notoriously suspicious of other duck species and decoy best to dedicated goldeneye spreads placed off windy, rocky points and deep-river breaks. Hunters must use heavy, high-contrast black-and-white decoys placed on longlines, as goldeneyes rarely commit to standard mallard or dabbler spreads.
lifespan: Up to 10–15 years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous; aquatic insects, crustaceans, mollusks, and small fish
habitat: Large lakes, rivers, coastal bays, and sheltered marine waters

description:
A large, streamlined fish duck with a long, narrow red bill lined with sharp, backward-pointing serrations. Drakes feature an uncrested bottle-green head, black back, immaculate white flanks, and a clean white breast that often carries a delicate, salmon-pink wash during the winter. Hens have an ash-gray body with a rich rusty-cinnamon crested head that transitions abruptly into a clean white throat.

Flies in fast, arrow-straight paths low over river channels and open reservoir surfaces, driven by rapid, shallow wing strokes that hold the bird's bill, head, and body in a rigid horizontal plane. Their flight lines are purposeful and low, rarely rising more than a few yards above the water. Generally silent on the wing, though hens produce a low, harsh croak when startled from river banks.

Common along clear, cold rivers, interior lakes, and coastal estuaries where they pursue baitfish. Because of their specialized fish diet, their meat carries a strong, unpalatable fishy flavor, leading most waterfowlers to pass on shooting them in favor of table-quality ducks. When encountered on rivers, they provide challenging, fast-crossing target presentations, but hunters should identify them early to avoid harvesting birds they do not intend to consume.
lifespan: Up to 13 years in the wild
diet: Primarily carnivorous; small fish, aquatic insects, amphibians, and crustaceans
habitat: Clear rivers, mountain streams, large lakes, and coastal estuaries
nesting_season: April to June (tree cavities or ground hollows)

description: A monomorphic, stocky, compact goose featuring dense silvery-blue plumage scalloped with black and white edges, a snow-white head and hindneck, a black throat, a small pinkish bill, and bright yellow-orange legs. Both sexes share identical plumage characteristics year-round, displaying a thick, well-insulated body built for harsh maritime climates. The contrast between the pure white head and black throat makes them instantly recognizable on coastal flats. Low-level fliers that cruise along wave-washed rocky beaches, coastal shoals, and tidal mudflats, beating their wings with rapid, stiff strokes. Their flight pattern is heavy and direct, keeping them low to the water as they navigate between rocky feeding points. They vocalize with sharp, rolling, metallic calls, which sound noticeably harsher than the calls of other northern geese. Restricted to the maritime fringes of coastal Alaska and the Bering Sea, feeding on intertidal seaweeds and eelgrass. Legal hunting is strictly regulated through a limited-entry drawing permit system for Alaska residents and subsistence hunters, with the season closing immediately when harvest quotas are reached. Outside of Alaska, they are fully protected, making them a rare, highly specialized game bird tied strictly to subarctic shores.
lifespan: 10–15 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; intertidal eelgrass, algae, salt-marsh grasses, and mollusks
habitat: Arctic coastal beaches, rocky marine shores, and tidal flats
conservation_status: Near Threatened (Protected across most of its range)

description:
A slender, long-legged whistling duck cloaked in warm, golden tawny-buff plumage, sporting a dark slate-blue bill, long blue-gray legs, and distinctive creamy-white side stripes that drape over the flanks. Unlike black-bellied whistling ducks, their wings are entirely dark blackish-brown above and below, broken only by a clean white crescent across the upper tail coverts. Both sexes share identical plumage characteristics year-round.

Maintains a slow, deliberate flight profile characterized by broad, rounded wings and long legs that extend prominently beyond the tail. Airborne birds vocalize with a clear, two-syllable squealing whistle sounding like "k-zee" or "whee-ow", which lacks the rattling chatter of the black-bellied species. They fly in loose, buoyant groups that make wide, circling approaches over agricultural fields.

Heavily tied to flooded agricultural rice prairies, coastal marshes, and shallow southern wetlands. They tend to be late migrants in the spring and early to depart in the autumn, decoy easily to gentle whistle imitations, and are celebrated for mild, high-quality table fare. Spreads set along shallow rice field checks or flooded pastures will pull them in cleanly without the need for aggressive calling.
lifespan: Up to 10 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; seeds, rice, grasses, and aquatic plant tubers
habitat: Flooded rice fields, shallow freshwater marshes, and shallow lakes

description:
A sleek, medium-sized puddle duck, the drake "gray duck" displays subtle, finely vermiculated gray body plumage, a steep forehead, a jet-black rump, and a dark bill. In the air, both sexes are instantly identified by a prominent, rectangular white speculum patch on the inner wing bordered by black and chestnut coverts, contrasting against a clean, snow-white belly. Hens resemble small, slim hen mallards but sport an orange-bordered bill and the diagnostic white wing speculum.

Fast and level fliers that travel in tight, compact flocks, frequently shifting altitude together and circling setups cautiously out of gun range. Drakes utter a unique, nasal, two-syllable "kack-kack" or reedy croak paired with a high-pitched whistle, while hens give a softer, higher-pitched, and slightly faster quack than a hen mallard. In flight, the flashing white speculum is visible even when the birds are viewed from above or behind.

Highly opportunistic vegetation feeders that frequently skirt the outside edges of decoy spreads without committing directly to the pocket. Because they do not respond well to loud, aggressive mallard hail calls, hunters find the best success using soft gadwall nasal calls, mallard feed chuckles, and wigeon whistles. Setting decoys in loose, scattered groups with plenty of open landing room helps encourage these cautious birds to slide within range.
lifespan: 5–12 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; aquatic plants, seeds, stems, and occasional aquatic insects
habitat: Shallow freshwater marshes, prairie potholes, lakes, and estuaries

description:
A stout, heavy-bodied diving duck, the drake displays a rounded head with a green iridescent gloss, a heavy black breast, white vermiculated back, and a broad blue-gray bill tipped with a wide black nail. In the air, both sexes show a bold white wing stripe that extends the entire length of the secondaries and runs well out into the outer primary flight feathers. Hens are warm brown with a prominent, clean white patch encircling the base of the bill.

Flocks form expansive, densely packed "bluebill" rafts that sweep down over the water with tremendous momentum, generating a distinct rushing-air roar on their final descent into decoys. Their wing action is swift and powerful, keeping flocks tightly clustered as they bank hard over open water. Vocalizations are minimal in flight, consisting of low, raspy purrs and gutter croaks.

Favors large open waters, coastal sounds, Great Lakes shoals, and saltwater bays rather than interior freshwater marshes. Hunters verify Greater Scaup in hand by confirming the white wing stripe runs through the primary flight feathers and that the bill nail is broad and wide, which is critical for complying with aggregate scaup bag limits. Layout boats and open-water blinds anchored over extensive mussel shoals provide the most productive hunting opportunities.
lifespan: Up to 18 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; mollusks, crustaceans, aquatic insects, and plant tubers
habitat: Large lakes, open bays, coastal marine waters, and estuaries

description:
A small, sleek diver, the drake is marked by an expansive, fan-shaped white crest bordered in jet-black, which can be raised or collapsed against the head. The drake's body is accented by two vertical black bars crossing a bright white breast, rich cinnamon-tawny flanks, and bright yellow eyes. Hens are small and dark brown, carrying a bushy, ragged reddish-cinnamon crest and dark brown eyes.

Lightning-fast fliers that negotiate narrow timber breaks and winding river channels with incredible maneuverability, flying with rapid, silent wingbeats. Their low-level flight allows them to dart through flooded woods without clipping tree limbs. Drakes utter a unique, frog-like rolling croak or purr during winter, while hens produce a raspy squawk when flushed.

Prefers secluded forested wetlands, beaver ponds, blackwater swamps, and quiet river oxbows alongside wood ducks. While their meat is generally not favored for the table due to a diet of small fish and aquatic bugs, fully plumaged drakes are highly prized by waterfowlers for decorative taxidermy mounts. They frequently drop into wood duck spreads, giving timber hunters fast, unexpected shooting opportunities.
lifespan: Up to 8–10 years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous; small fish, aquatic insects, crayfish, and aquatic amphibians
habitat: Wooded swamps, forested rivers, beaver ponds, and quiet sloughs

description:
Slightly smaller and more compact than the Greater Scaup, the drake's head exhibits an angular peak at the rear of the crown and shows a purplish gloss under direct sunlight. Its white wing stripe is strictly confined to the secondary flight feathers, fading to a dusky brownish-gray across the outer primaries. The bill is light blue-gray with a narrow, small black nail at the tip; hens display brown bodies with white feathering ringing the bill base.

Famous for dramatic, vertical descents from cruising altitude, dropping out of the sky in tight, buzzing packs before leveling out just feet above the decoys. The sound of a large flock descending has been compared to tearing canvas, generated by the air shearing against their stiff wing feathers. Drakes emit low wheezing purrs, while hens utter a harsh, raspy "scaup-scaup" call when startled or flying.

The predominant bluebill of interior marshes, rivers, and prairie potholes, staging in huge numbers during late autumn cold fronts. Successful spreads require long strings of high-contrast black-and-white floating decoys deployed on longlines along deep channels or points. Because bag limits are often restricted to one or two birds, hunters must practice separating them from redheads and ringnecks on fast crossing passes.
lifespan: Up to 18 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; aquatic insects, mollusks, crustaceans, and plant seeds
habitat: Lakes, ponds, rivers, marshes, and sheltered coastal bays

description:
A small, slender, and highly vocal sea duck, winter drakes sport a striking piebald plumage of snow-white, slate-gray, and black, complete with a pink-banded black bill and exceptionally long, needle-like central tail feathers. Hens lack the long tail and have a warm-brown and white patterned head and back. Both sexes fly with completely dark wings that lack any white speculum markings, providing a clean silhouette over the water.

Blistering fast fliers that erratically tilt, bank, and roll from side to side in flight, flashing alternating white bellies and dark backs mere inches above rolling swells. Their speed and erratic flight patterns make them one of the most challenging targets in waterfowl hunting. They are among the most vocal of all waterfowl, filling cold maritime bays with their melodious, yodeling calls sounding like 'caloo-caloo' or 'south-south-southerly'.

Legendary divers capable of foraging on crustaceans at depths exceeding 150 feet. Targeting them requires setting layout boats or seaward blinds near deep current rips and open ocean drop-offs, swinging aggressively through their erratic, high-speed flight paths. Hunters must use heavy leads and shoot well out in front of crossing birds, as their airspeed consistently outpaces expectations.
size: Length 38–55 cm (15–22 inches excluding tail streamers)
lifespan: Up to 15–20 years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous; benthic crustaceans, small fish, mollusks, and marine worms
habitat: Arctic marine waters, open ocean bays, deep lakes, and coastal surf zones
conservation_status: Vulnerable / Least Concern (Population decline noted in some regions)

description:
The continental benchmark for puddle ducks, drakes carry an iridescent emerald-green head, crisp white neck collar, chestnut breast, and an upward-curled central black tail feather. Both sexes display a brilliant violet-blue speculum bordered on both leading and trailing edges by clean white bars, which flashes vividly during banking turns. In early season or eclipse plumage, drakes resemble mottled-brown hens but can be separated in hand or at close range by their solid dull-yellowish bill, unlike the dark, orange-splotched bill of the hen.

Mallards launch vertically from the surface on powerful wingbeats, cruising in deliberate, wide-circling flight paths while scouting marsh openings and flooded agricultural fields. Acoustic dimorphism is stark: hens deliver the classic, loud, raspy decrescendo "quack" and long-distance hail calls that standard duck calls emulate, while airborne drakes emit only low, raspy, single-syllable "kwek" or "yeeb" whistles.

Wary and easily educated by hunting pressure, birds flare instantly from unnatural movement, blind shine, or off-beat calling, making spinning-wing decoys and realistic water motion critical on still mornings. In mixed-bag regions, hunters must confirm the double white wing bars and pale belly to avoid mistakenly taking darker American Black Ducks or Mottled Ducks against single-bird bag limits. Clean decoy spreads, disciplined calling cadences, and total concealment are fundamental to consistent success.
lifespan: 5–10 years in the wild (can exceed 20 years)
diet: Omnivorous; seeds, grains, aquatic vegetation, insects, and small fish
habitat: Freshwater marshes, ponds, rivers, agricultural fields, and urban parks

description:
Exhibiting intermediate phenotypes between both parent stocks, these birds typically show an overall dark body with a dusky head that carries an irregular green wash across the crown and eye stripe. The wing speculum is generally dark violet-blue, but unlike a pure black duck, it often displays a thin, broken white border along the trailing edge and trace white tipping on the leading edge. Bill color is often a muddy greenish-yellow on drakes, occasionally showing faint black gape spots.

Leaps abruptly off the water with identical vertical agility to wild mallards, flying in direct, strong lines with whistling wing feathers and pale underwing surfaces. Flocks travel with the same purposeful cadence as pure puddle ducks, readily mixing into flights of either parent species. Vocalizations fall directly in line with pure mallard cadences, with hens delivering standard resonant quacks and drakes emitting reedy rasps.

Extremely common along coastal estuaries and river deltas where mallards and black ducks overlap on breeding ranges. Hunters must inspect harvested birds closely in hand, as wildlife officers evaluate speculum border bars, body plumage saturation, and bill tone to apply the bird toward either the restrictive black duck daily limit or the standard mallard limit. Keeping track of regional enforcement standards on hybrids ensures that hunters stay on the correct side of their daily bag limits.
lifespan: 5–10 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; seeds, aquatic plants, grains, insects, and small invertebrates
habitat: Coastal marshes, tidal estuaries, river deltas, and freshwater wetlands
conservation_status: Not separately evaluated (Protected/managed under parent species limits)

description:
Both drakes and hens closely resemble oversized, richly saturated hen mallards, covered in dark, warm-brown scalloped plumage with a paler buff head and throat. The speculum flashes greenish-blue to deep blue, bordered by narrow black bars and only trace white tips along the trailing edge. Drakes are readily distinguished in hand and at close range by their solid olive-green to yellowish bills, while females possess pale orange bills marked with dusky splotches.

Flushes vertically from narrow desert river corridors, stock ponds, and agricultural irrigation ditches, flying with the steady, authoritative cadence of northern mallards. Their flight lines are strong and deliberate, showing pale underwings that contrast against their rich, dark body feathering. Hens produce loud, coarse quacking series, while drakes utilize the low-pitched, quiet rasp characteristic of the genus Anas.

Formerly classified as a mallard subspecies, it is now recognized as a distinct species native to the southwestern border states and northern Mexico. Hunters in the Rio Grande basin and desert southwest must exercise caution when hunting zones with aggregate hen-mallard restrictions, checking bill color and speculum borders to confirm species identity. Small spreads of mallard or pintail decoys placed on shallow desert stock tanks produce steady shooting during the winter months.
lifespan: 5–10 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; seeds, grains, aquatic plants, and aquatic invertebrates
habitat: Desert streams, mountain rivers, stock ponds, and agricultural marshes

description:
A large, warm-buff to dark-brown dabbler resembling a pale hen mallard or a faded black duck, characterized by an unstreaked buffy throat and pale face. The speculum shines iridescent blue-green with black trailing margins and totally lacks white border bars, though a faint white line on the trailing edge can occasionally appear in worn plumage. Drakes possess a solid bright yellow-olive bill accented by a distinct black spot at the gape, while hens have duller orange-yellow bills with dark blotches.

Moves in low, watchful pairs or small family groups just above coastal cordgrass and flooded rice impoundments, seldom forming massive mixed flocks. Their flight is measured and vigilant, keeping them low to the grass as they navigate marsh systems. Vocalizations closely mirror mallards, with females delivering loud, descending quacks and males sounding soft, reedy chuckles.

Primarily non-migratory residents of Gulf Coast and southern coastal marshes. Due to declining populations and hybridization pressures, they carry tight harvest caps or total season closures in specific zones, meaning gunners must never shoot at dark-bodied ducks in low light without confirming the lack of white speculum bars and the pale buff throat. Setting small, scattered spreads in secluded marsh potholes is the most effective way to coax these resident birds within range.
lifespan: 5–10 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; seeds, aquatic vegetation, snails, insects, and small crustaceans
habitat: Coastal marshes, brackish estuaries, flooded rice fields, and coastal prairies

description: A monomorphic, slender, streamlined upland game bird with soft brownish-gray body plumage, black spots on the wing coverts, a pinkish-buff wash on the breast, and a long, sharply pointed tail bordered by white outer feathers. Both sexes share similar plumage, though males exhibit an iridescent pinkish-rose wash on the sides of the neck. The legs are small and coral-pink, and the bill is slender and dark. Extremely fast and acrobatic fliers that regularly reach fifty-five miles per hour, producing a sharp whistling sound with their wings during takeoff. In flight, they execute sudden, erratic barrel rolls, dives, and flares that challenge gunners. On the ground, males sound a familiar, mournful five-note coo sound though they remain silent during rapid pass-shooting flights. The traditional opening-day quarry across North American agricultural fields, hunted over harvested sunflowers, millet, wheat stubble, and evening watering holes. Their small profile and erratic flight require fast swing speeds and open chokes like improved cylinder or skeet firing light target loads of #7.5 or #8 shot. Stationary motorized decoys with spinning wings mounted on stakes are exceptionally effective at drawing passing doves into close range.
lifespan: 1.5 years average in wild (max recorded over 19 years)
diet: Granivorous; agricultural grains, weed seeds, and occasional insects
habitat: Open country, agricultural fields, prairies, woodland edges, and suburban areas

description:
An exceptionally sleek, long-necked dabbler, the drake pintail boasts a chocolate-brown head, a bright white neck stripe extending up from a snow-white chest, and elongated, needle-like black central tail feathers. In flight, their long, slender necks and pointed wings produce a gull-like, hydrodynamic silhouette that cannot be mistaken for any other duck. The speculum is an iridescent dark greenish-bronze bordered by a rust-tan leading bar and a crisp white trailing edge.

Pintails fly high, fast, and gracefully, sliding down from altitude in long, sweeping, cautious spirals that inspect every inch of a marsh before setting their wings. Their wing strokes are narrow and swept-back, giving them a distinct dart-like appearance on long crossing passes. Drakes rarely quack, instead emitting a soft, two-note flute-like whistle sounding like "wheet-wheet", while hens produce a low, hoarse, dry croak.

Renowned as one of the most decoy-shy ducks in North America, often circling a spread half a dozen times before landing well outside the decoys. High-visibility sprig decoys with prominent white chests, minimal motion-decoy flash on clear days, and conservative whistling are essential to finishing them within range under strict single-bird or two-bird bag limits. Spreads deployed in open sheetwater or wide, flooded agricultural basins yield the best results.
lifespan: Up to 15–20 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; seeds, aquatic plants, grains, insects, and small snails
habitat: Open wetlands, marshes, agricultural fields, and shallow coastal bays

description:
Instantly identified by an enormous, spoon-shaped black bill that is longer than the head and lined with fine, comb-like filtering lamellae. Prime drakes are vividly marked with an iridescent dark green head, brilliant white chest, rich chestnut-red belly and flanks, and pale blue shoulder patches on the wings. Hens are mottled brown with a heavy, orange-edged spoon bill and pale blue forewing patches.

Flocks fly with steady, measured wingbeats, maintaining a distinct silhouette that appears front-heavy and down-angled due to the heavy bill. They are surprisingly nimble when banking, occasionally dropping out of the sky with sudden side-slips into shallow marsh holes. Drakes emit a low, guttural, rhythmic clucking sounding like "thook-thook" or "clook", while hens produce a muted, nasal quack.

Nicknamed "spoonbills" or "bootlips," they feed by sweeping their bills across the water surface to filter micro-invertebrates and seeds from stagnant marsh pools and mudflats. They decoy very readily into almost any puddle duck spread without requiring calling, though their table quality varies widely depending on whether they have been feeding on seeds or aquatic invertebrates. They provide excellent shooting practice over shallow impoundments, dropping willingly into standard decoy layouts.
lifespan: Up to 10–15 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; zooplankton, micro-invertebrates, seeds, and aquatic plants
habitat: Shallow freshwater marshes, prairie ponds, mudflats, and estuaries

description:
A slender diving sawbill featuring a shaggy, double-pointed crest on the back of the head, bright red eyes, and a very thin, slightly upturned serrated red bill. Drakes sport a dark green crested head, a white neck collar, a reddish-brown breast streaked with dark spots, and black-and-white patterned wings. Hens display a ragged crest, dull gray-brown plumage, and a cinnamon head that blends gradually into a pale neck.

Rapid, bullet-like fliers that skim across open coastal waters in single-file lines, generating tremendous forward airspeed with stiff, shallow wing strokes. Their flight silhouette is elongated and arrow-straight, with head, neck, and body aligned in a single horizontal plane. They emit low, rasping grunts during courtship displays, but remain largely mute on the wing.

Primarily a bird of open saltwater bays, tidal sounds, and ocean beaches, contrasting with the freshwater preference of the Common Merganser. They are taken mostly as incidental birds by sea-duck hunters, as their fish-based diet similarly renders them unappealing for culinary use. When encountered along coastal points, their high flight speeds require assertive shooting leads and wide follow-throughs.
lifespan: Up to 9–14 years in the wild
diet: Primarily carnivorous; small fish, aquatic insects, crustaceans, and frogs
habitat: Marine bays, coastal estuaries, saltwater inlets, and large freshwater lakes
nesting_season: May to July (ground nests hidden under vegetation)

description:
A medium-sized diving duck with a high, rounded, bulbous head profile that contrasts with the sloping wedge of the Canvasback. Drakes feature a bright copper-red head, black chest, dark ash-gray back, and a light blue bill tipped in black and separated by a crisp white band. Hens are uniform warm-brown with a faint pale patch at the base of a similarly patterned blue, black, and white bill.

Highly social birds that fly in dense, churning flocks that undulate low over the water, banking sharply as a single mass before sliding into decoy spreads on cupped wings. Flocks maneuver with a characteristic sweeping motion, turning together with tight precision. Drakes produce an unusual cat-like meow or groan sounding like "whee-oow" during courtship, while flying hens emit hoarse, vibrating squawks.

Gregarious divers that decoy with reckless abandon, frequently pitching directly into large spreads of bluebill or canvasback decoys anchored over coastal seagrass flats. Hunters must separate drakes from Canvasbacks in flight by noting the Redhead's rounder head, darker gray back, and shorter, banded blue bill. Setting spreads of high-contrast diving duck decoys on open bays or lagoon shallows provides consistent shooting during late-season pushes.
lifespan: Up to 15–20 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; aquatic plants, roots, seeds, aquatic insects, and small snails
habitat: Shallow lakes, bays, marshes, and coastal lagoons
source: docx (image names from chat drafts, not yet confirmed)

description:
Despite its name, which refers to an obscure chestnut neck band visible only in hand, this medium diver is recognized by the drake's glossy purplish-black head, jet-black back, bright white vertical flank crescent, and slate-blue bill banded with two bold white rings. Hens are grayish-brown with a white eyering, a pale bill-base wash, and a matching white-banded bill. In flight, both sexes show a uniform, dark slate-gray speculum rather than a white wing stripe.

Rocket-fast fliers that drop into decoys with a distinct whistling or ripping air sound, maneuvering through tight spaces with agility uncommon among diving ducks. They drop out of high altitudes in steep dives, leveling out over timber holes with remarkable aerial control. Drakes produce soft hissing purrs, while hens emit low, grating growls when flushing.

Known colloquially as the "ringbill" or "blackjack," they heavily utilize shallow forested swamps, beaver ponds, and lily-pad marshes alongside puddle ducks. They decoy eagerly to regular mallard and wood duck spreads, making them a common bonus bird in flooded timber. Hunters need not invest in specialized diver spreads, as ringnecks routinely pitch into small woodland potholes holding only half a dozen floating puddle duck blocks.
lifespan: Up to 10–14 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; aquatic plant tubers, seeds, aquatic insects, snails, and small fish
habitat: Wooded swamps, freshwater marshes, beaver ponds, and shallow lakes
source: docx (image names from chat drafts, not yet confirmed)

description: This monomorphic goose resembles a miniature white-phase Snow Goose, measuring only slightly larger than a mallard, with pure white plumage and black primary wingtips. It is separated from the Snow Goose by its short, stubby, triangular pink bill that completely lacks a black grinning patch, meeting the face in a straight, vertical line often covered in blueish-gray warty caruncles. Blue-morph Ross's geese exist but are exceptionally rare across all flyways. Highly agile fliers that use rapid, choppy wing strokes, executing remarkable aerial slips and barrel rolls into decoys among larger mixed flocks. Their wing cadence is faster than that of snow geese, allowing them to shift positions rapidly within large swirling flocks. Their call is a distinct, high-pitched squeak or grunt sounding like "keek" or "kug", which is higher and weaker than a snow goose bark. Migrates alongside snow geese through the Central and Pacific flyways, feeding on grain and short green grasses in agricultural basins. Hunters targeting light geese identify them in hand by the short bill length, lack of a smiling patch, and small body frame. During spring conservation orders, they are harvested alongside snow geese over large electronic caller spreads, decoying cleanly to realistic windsock layouts.
lifespan: 8–15 years in the wild
diet: Herbivorous; grasses, sedges, roots, and agricultural grains
habitat: Arctic tundra, agricultural fields, wet meadows, and marshes

description:
A small, thick-set stifftail duck with a short, thick neck, a scoop-shaped bill, and stiff, spiky tail feathers that are frequently fanned and cocked upright while swimming. In autumn and winter, drakes lose their famous rust-red plumage and sky-blue bills, becoming drab gray-brown with dark caps and bright white cheek patches. Hens are similarly dull brown but have a distinct dark stripe running horizontally across their whitish cheek.

Extremely reluctant to take flight, choosing to escape danger by sinking down into the water or diving smoothly beneath the surface. When forced into the air, their tiny wings beat with a blur-like buzzing cadence, keeping them skimming mere inches above the water surface in straight, unswerving lines. Flocks rarely form in the air, with most flights consisting of low-skimming singles or pairs.

Inhabits open, deep-water marshes, reservoirs, and coastal bays where they raft in compact groups over submerged weeds. They rarely commit to standard decoy layouts, usually encountered as fast-moving singles buzzing the outer lines of open-water blinds. Hunters targeting divers generally pass on them, though their speed provides a brief, challenging crossing presentation when they buzz blind locations.
lifespan: Up to 5–8 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; midge larvae, aquatic insects, seeds, and aquatic plant roots
habitat: Freshwater lakes, deep marshes, prairie potholes, and sheltered bays
source: docx (image names from chat drafts, not yet confirmed)

description: A monomorphic, tall, long-legged wetland and upland game bird featuring ash-gray body plumage often stained reddish-brown from iron-rich marsh mud, a bushy bustle over the tail, a long, spear-like bill, and a bare patch of crimson skin across the crown. Immature birds lack the red crown and display pale buff-brown heads and necks. Standing over four feet tall, their imposing ground profile cannot be confused with any other North American quarry. Flocks cruise at high altitudes in long lines or V-formations, flying with their long necks fully extended forward and their long legs trailing straight out behind. Their wingbeat is distinctive, featuring a brisk, energetic upstroke that looks flicked upward rather than stroked downward. Flocks communicate with rolling, rattling, trumpet-like bugles that carry across multiple miles of open agricultural country. Revered as the "ribeye of the sky" for phenomenal meat quality that resembles prime beef tenderloin. They possess exceptional eyesight and feed in open grain fields, requiring dedicated full-body crane decoys, absolute camouflage in A-frame or layout blinds, and careful shooting at vitals. Hunters must hide blinds along natural fence lines or ditch banks, as cranes will skirt any abnormal structure placed in open stubble fields.
size: Height 80–120 cm (31–47 inches); Length 85–100 cm (33–39 inches)
lifespan: 15–20 years in the wild (can exceed 20–30 years)
diet: Omnivorous; grains, seeds, berries, insects, small rodents, frogs, and reptiles
habitat: Freshwater marshes, wet meadows, bogs, and agricultural crop fields

description: A dimorphic species occurring in two distinct color phases: the Snow morph is pure white with jet-black primary wingtips, while the Blue morph features a slate-gray body, dark wings, and a contrasting snow-white head and neck. Both phases possess a heavy, pink bill equipped with a prominent black grinning patch along the cutting edge that is visible at close range. Intermediates showing varied white and slate body patches are also common in field spreads. Travels in massive flocks comprising thousands of birds, forming towering, swirling tornadoes that drop from tremendous altitudes toward feeding grounds. Their flight is loud, chaotic, and continuous, with birds constantly shifting positions as they circle downward. Flocks generate a deafening wall of sound consisting of high-pitched, barking yelps, screams, and single-syllable squawks. Overabundant populations that damage subarctic breeding tundra have led to liberal Spring Conservation Orders featuring electronic callers, unplugged shotguns, and no bag limits. Success requires massive spreads of 500 to 2,000+ windsock or rotary decoys placed in agricultural fields along migration corridors. Scouting roosts and setting up on hot feeding fields under overcast, windy conditions yields the highest success rates.
lifespan: 10–15 years in the wild (record up to 20+ years)
diet: Herbivorous; roots, rhizomes, grasses, sedges, and agricultural grains
habitat: Arctic tundra, agricultural fields, coastal marshes, and wet meadows
conservation_status: Least Concern (Overabundant populations managed via special hunts)

description: A monomorphic, compact, rounded marsh bird with a stubby, chicken-like bright yellow bill, an olive-brown back streaked with white lines, a slate-gray breast, and a black mask running from the bill across the face and throat. The short tail is frequently cocked, showing clean white undertail coverts. Their legs are yellowish-green and equipped with long, unwebbed toes designed for walking across floating marsh grasses. Flushes only under direct pressure, rising from the emergent cover with a weak, fluttering flight pattern, dangling its yellowish-green legs before collapsing back into the vegetation after a short glide. Their flights rarely cover more than twenty or thirty yards, keeping them low to the marsh grass. Highly vocal in the marsh, producing a sharp 'keek' alarm note and a distinctive, high-pitched descending whinny. Pursued alongside Virginia Rails during early autumn flood-tide stages in wild rice marshes and coastal cordgrass flats. Because their flight is brief and erratic, hunters must be ready to shoulder and shoot instantly with open-choked shotguns before the bird disappears back into the marsh canopy. Pushing flat-bottom rail skiffs through flooded marsh grass with long poles is the traditional and most effective method of harvest.
lifespan: 3–5 years in the wild
diet: Omnivorous; seeds of marsh plants, aquatic insects, snails, and small crustaceans
habitat: Freshwater marshes, wetlands, flooded meadows, and rice paddies

description:
Known by maritime hunters as the "skunkhead," the drake is solid velvety black accented by a stark white patch on the forehead and a long triangular white patch on the back of the neck. Its bill is massive, swollen, and brightly patterned in red, yellow, white, and a distinct black patch on the side. Hens are dark brown with two fuzzy white patches on each side of the face and a pale patch on the nape.

Powerful, direct fliers that buzz low over ocean breaking zones in strung-out, single-file lines that rise and fall with the rolling surf. Their heavy bodies require steady wingbeats to maintain momentum over coastal waters. They are generally silent in flight, but their stiff wingbeats create a low, rhythmic whistling sound as they pass blinds set on ocean shoals.

Frequents rugged coastal surf lines, open bays, and ocean channels on both coasts, feeding heavily on clams, crabs, and mussels. They are exceptionally tough birds that decoy aggressively to high-contrast floating longlines, requiring heavy non-toxic shot payloads and tight choke patterns to fold birds cleanly. Layout boats anchored in ocean inlets or seaward points provide consistent shooting during the late fall migration.
lifespan: Up to 10–12 years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous; marine mollusks, clams, mussels, crabs, and aquatic insects
habitat: Coastal marine waters, ocean surf zones, bays, and large inland lakes

description:
This monomorphic swan is North America's largest native waterfowl, weighing twenty to thirty pounds with wingspans reaching eight feet, covered entirely in pure white plumage. The all-black bill is long and massive, forming an unbroken, straight V-profile running from the bill tip directly into the eye and forehead without any notched indentation, and lacking any yellow facial markings. Immature birds are dusky gray with pinkish tones centered on their black-edged bills.

Majestic in flight, beating its massive wings with slow, deep, resonant power that carries long flight lines across northern waterways. Their long necks are held completely straight in flight, balanced by heavy, dark feet tucked under the tail. Their call is a loud, resonant, low-pitched brassy bugle sounding like 'ko-hoh', resembling the sound of an orchestral trumpet across the marsh.

Protected throughout almost all of its continental range following long-term restoration efforts. In states that offer legal Tundra Swan hunting, waterfowlers must confirm the bill profile, facial skin boundary, and vocal pitch to avoid shooting a protected Trumpeter Swan. Carrying quality optics to verify the straight V-line of the bill and listening for the low brassy horn call prevents accidental illegal harvest.
wingspan: 185–210 cm (73–83 inches) to over 240 cm (94 inches)
lifespan: 12–20 years in the wild (can exceed 24–30 years)
diet: Herbivorous; submerged aquatic vegetation, roots, tubers, and grasses
habitat: Large shallow lakes, ponds, slow rivers, and coastal wetlands
conservation_status: Least Concern / Recovered (Strictly protected or regulated)

description:
A monomorphic. large, graceful waterfowl cloaked entirely in snowy-white plumage, balanced by an all-black bill, legs, and feet. The bill meets the forehead at a sharp, abrupt angle below the eye, and mature adults usually carry a small, distinct yellow spot on the black skin directly in front of the eye. Immature birds show mottled gray-brown plumage with paler, pinkish bills during their first autumn flight south.

High-altitude fliers that travel in stately, disciplined V-formations or long diagonal lines driven by deep, powerful, rhythmic wing strokes. Their flight is fluid and effortless, covering immense distances between Arctic breeding grounds and coastal wintering bays. They vocalize continuously with high-pitched, barking bugle notes and whistle-like cries sounding like 'kloo-kloo', which can be heard long before the birds become visible.

Hunted strictly through limited-entry lottery tag systems in select Atlantic, Central, and Pacific flyway states. Hunters use large white swan decoys or modified white flags placed in flooded agricultural fields or coastal shallows, using heavy non-toxic shot like T, BBB, or BB on broad crossing shots. Because their size makes them appear closer than they are, gunners should wait until facial details are visible before pulling the trigger.
lifespan: 10–20 years in the wild (record over 20 years)
diet: Herbivorous; aquatic plants, roots, tubers, stems, and leftover grains
habitat: Arctic tundra, shallow lakes, estuaries, bays, and flooded agricultural fields

description:
A monomorphic. small, laterally compressed marsh bird built to slip between dense stems of cordgrass, featuring rich rusty-red breast plumage, barred black-and-white flanks, a dark crown, and a slightly downcurved, slender reddish-orange bill. Legs are long and reddish, and the short tail is often held cocked upright. Their compressed body allows them to sprint through dense marsh vegetation without displacing cover.

Extremely reluctant to take wing, preferring to run through dense marsh vegetation like a rodent. When flushed, they flutter weakly just above the tops of the reeds with their legs dangling awkwardly below, flying only a short distance before dropping back into cover. They produce harsh, clicking grunts and metallic descending calls sounding like 'kid-ick, kid-ick' from deep inside tidal marsh grass.

Hunted along coastal tidal marshes and inland freshwater wetlands during extreme high tides. Gunners pole flat-bottom skiffs through flooded marsh cover, executing quick snap-shots with light target loads as birds briefly flush into the wind. Hunting during full-moon tides floods the upper marsh canopy, concentrating these secretive rails along narrow shoreline fringes where they are more easily flushed.
lifespan: 3–5 years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous and omnivorous; aquatic insects, beetles, snails, earthworms, and seeds
habitat: Freshwater and brackish marshes, freshwater wetlands, and dense reed beds

description:
A monomorphic medium-sized grayish-brown goose highlighted by a prominent patch of white feathers surrounding the base of the pink-orange bill and bold, irregular black bars across the belly. Legs are bright orange, and the tail is dark with a clean white tip and white upper coverts. Juvenile birds lack the white facial patch and black belly bars, showing uniform brown-gray underparts during early autumn hunts.

Exceptionally fast and nimble in the air, flying in disciplined lines or V-formations that break into spectacular, side-slipping tumbles when descending into fields. Flocks dump out of the sky with incredible agility, rocking side to side on set wings. They are famously vocal, identified by a distinct, high-pitched, musical laughing or yodeling call sounding like 'kah-lah-lah-luck' or 'ha-ha-ha'.

Highly prized by waterfowlers across the Mississippi, Central, and Pacific flyways as premier table fare. Fooling educated specks requires specialized, tuned specklebelly calls, high-end full-body decoys set in loose family groups, and absolute stillness in rice or bean stubble. Unlike Canada geese, specklebellies are easily flared by over-calling or harsh flagging, making subtle, realistic two-note yodels the best approach.
lifespan: 8–15 years in the wild (record over 20 years)
diet: Herbivorous; grasses, sedges, roots, and agricultural grains
habitat: Arctic tundra, agricultural fields, wet meadows, and river floodplains

description:
This monomorphic dove is larger and heavier-bodied than the Mourning Dove, characterized by a rounded tail with white corner tips, a bare patch of sky-blue skin surrounding dark eyes, and a bold white crescent along the leading wing edge that expands into a striking white bar across the wing in flight. The body is brownish-gray with a slight purplish-pink cast across the neck and breast on breeding males.

Flight paths are linear, smooth, and predictable compared to the zig-zagging maneuvers of Mourning Doves, traveling in steady flocks between agricultural fields and roosting timber. Their wingbeats are rhythmic and steady, giving them a more direct, purposeful appearance in the air. Their call is a distinctive, rhythmic four-note coo often transcribed as 'who-cooks-for-you'.

Concentrated across the desert Southwest, Texas, and Gulf Coast regions, feeding heavily on grain, citrus, and weed seeds. They provide consistent shooting along field margins and irrigation corridors, easily separated from Mourning Doves in flight by their square tails and prominent white wing bars. Hunters set up along tree lines and grain borders, pass-shooting steady flights during morning and late-afternoon feeding flights.
lifespan: Up to 7 years in the wild
diet: Granivorous and frugivorous; agricultural grains, weed seeds, cactus fruit, and berries
habitat: Desert scrub, arid woodlands, citrus groves, and suburban parks

description:
The largest of the three North American scoters, drakes are dark brownish-black with a swollen orange bill, a small white teardrop crescent flicking upward from the rear of the eye, and an expansive, square white speculum on the wings. Hens are dark soot-brown with faint white facial spots, but they share the same unmistakable white speculum on the wing. Their bills are heavy and wide, adapted for crushing hard-shelled mollusks.

Heavy, lumbering fliers that require a running start across the surface to get airborne, settling into long, straight flight paths low over the water while flashing their bright white wing patches on every stroke. Flocks travel in long, single-file chains that stay low to the waves, rarely climbing high above open sounds. In flight, they produce low, guttural croaking sounds, but are otherwise quiet.

Hardiest of the sea ducks, wintering in cold northern saltwater, broad sounds, and large open bodies of freshwater like the Great Lakes. The bold white speculum makes them identifiable at great distances, helping gunners confirm the species before committing to shots over deep-water rigs. Setting heavy longlines over open-water mussel beds and using dense shot loads ensures clean harvests over rolling ocean swells.
lifespan: Up to 10–15 years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous; marine mollusks, clams, mussels, crustaceans, and snails
habitat: Coastal marine bays, estuaries, ocean surf, and large inland lakes
conservation_status: Least Concern / Vulnerable (Declining trends in some localized populations)

description:
A small, cryptically colored game bird featuring buff and dark-brown longitudinal stripes down the head and back, barred flanks, short legs, and an extraordinarily long, straight, slender bill with a flexible, sensitive tip used for probing mud. In hand, their plumage provides exceptional camouflage against saturated soils and marsh grasses. The breast is mottled buff, and the underbelly is clean white.

When flushed, they explode from muddy cover with tremendous speed, uttering a harsh, raspy alarm call sounding like 'scaip-scaip', before executing a series of wild, unpredictable zig-zagging aerial evasions. They climb steeply into the wind and level off at high altitudes; during spring courtship, they perform aerial dives that create a hollow, humming 'winnowing' sound using specialized outer tail feathers.

Hunted on saturated pastures, exposed mudflats, and boggy marsh edges where their long bills can probe for earthworms and larvae. Their erratic zig-zagging flight flummoxes inexperienced gunners; the most effective strategy is to wait out the initial two or three erratic turns, mounting and firing once the bird levels off on a stable flight trajectory. Walking upwind through muddy ground keeps flushes within reasonable shotgun range.
lifespan: Up to 8–9 years in the wild
diet: Carnivorous and insectivorous; earthworms, insect larvae, beetles, and small aquatic invertebrates
habitat: Saturated meadows, bogs, muddy river edges, and wet pastures

description:
A compact, highly ornate tree duck, the drake features an iridescent green and purple crested head with white bridle lines, a red eye, a multi-colored red, white, and yellow bill, and a rich burgundy-wine breast. Hens are sleek gray-brown with a teardrop-shaped white patch around the eye and a subtle blue-green sheen on the wings. In flight, both sexes show a long, square, dark tail and dark underwings with contrasting white belly lines.

Masters of timber navigation, they cut through dense forest canopies and flooded bottomland hardwoods with unmatched speed, banking sharply around tree trunks with their heads held high and bills angled downward. Their flight is darting and low, weaving through tight tree branches effortlessly. They are exceptionally vocal on the wing: hens emit a piercing, rising squeal sounding like "oo-eek! oo-eek!", while drakes make a softer, high-pitched finch-like whistle sounding like "jheep".

Inhabitants of beaver ponds, river oxbows, and cypress-tupelo swamps, they feed heavily on wild acorns and smartweed. Shooting is intense, fast, and close-quarters during legal shooting light at dawn and dusk, requiring open-choked shotguns and rapid target acquisition before birds vanish behind timber. Setting small spreads of half a dozen wood duck decoys in quiet river sloughs will bring incoming flights right into shooting range.
lifespan: Up to 3–4 years average in wild (some reach 6+ years)
diet: Omnivorous; acorns, beechnuts, seeds, aquatic plants, and aquatic insects
habitat: Wooded swamps, flooded timber, beaver ponds, and slow-moving wooded streams
conservation_status: Least Concern (Successfully recovered from historical overhunting via nest boxes)
